newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard forces land rights compromise.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard forces land rights compromise.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard moved on Monday to end a damaging brawl over conflicting land claims between Aborigines and farmers, saying he would ignore opposition from both sides and impose his own compromise.
Speaking after a special summit of state and territory leaders failed to resolve the row, Howard said he had raised the prospect of an early election to force his plan through.

The row over a December High Court decision giving Aborigines rights to land leased to farmers has split the community, driven a wedge between Howard's Liberal-National coalition and -- farmers and miners say -- damaged Australia's multi-billion dollar primary industries sector.
Howard said his compromise, which will cost an unknown amount in compensation to Aborigines, was the fairest and most practical solution for all sides.
"I am convinced that the 10-point plan of mine is the fairest, best, most practical way of delivering certainty and security to farmers and justice to the Aboriginal community," he said.

Key elements of the blueprint include confirming farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, but guaranteeing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
It also reduces Aboriginal rights to negotiate over development and other uses of land and exempts cities, towns and water catchments from Aboriginal claims.
State government leaders told reporters after the summit they had reservations about aspects of the compromise.

Queensland premier Rob Borbidge, who has led the fight to have Aboriginal "native title" extinguished, said there were "still certain legal and technical and administrative difficulties confronting the states".
"Queensland isn't in the deal, we have reserved our position," he added,
Howard said he had considered a possible early election over the issue. "I think in these sorts of discussions the full gamut of political possibilities is always canvassed," he said.

Under the constitution, a government can call an early election, followed by a joint sitting of parliament, to pass controversial legislation if the upper house Senate blocks reforms. Minority parties in the Senate have voiced opposition to aspects of the Howard plan.

Australia's High Court in 1992 declared Aborigines had native title rights over government-owned land, but a subsequent system to regulate native title assumed it did not extend to land let to pastoralists.
Last December, the High Court ruled that an undefined Aboriginal native title also existed on those pastoral leases.
Farmers and conservative politicians, some senior members of Howard's coalition, want native title done away with.

Howard said he would draft legislation implementing his plan after further talks with the states and territories, Aboriginal groups and farmers. But while there was room for some change, there would be no compromise on the plan's basic thrust.
"I won't consider amendments that alter the principles of the 10-point plan. This is not an ambit claim (negotiating position)," he said.
Howard has said up to 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square kms (2.96 million square miles) could be affected by Aboriginal land claims.
